claims.text: The baseline material is as-cast HfMoTaTiZr.
Baseline HfMoTaTiZr has a density of approximately 10.21 g/cm³.
Baseline HfMoTaTiZr has a room-temperature yield strength of about 1600 MPa.
Baseline HfMoTaTiZr has a yield strength of about 855 MPa at 1000 °C.
Baseline HfMoTaTiZr has greater than 50% room-temperature ductility.
Approximately 20% of the Hf should be replaced with Al.
Replacing Hf with Al will reduce the alloy's average atomic weight and density.
The Al-substituted alloy will retain a homogeneous single-phase BCC solid solution.
Al incorporation will maintain lattice distortion and bonding interactions comparable to those of baseline HfMoTaTiZr.
The retained lattice distortion and bonding interactions will preserve solid-solution strengthening and dislocation-mediated deformation.
Al substitution will preserve high yield strength and ductility at room temperature and around 1000 °C.
The approximately 20% Hf-to-Al substitution will reduce density by about 5–10% relative to the baseline.
Room-temperature and 1000 °C yield strengths will remain within approximately ±10% of the baseline values.
Room-temperature and 1000 °C ductility will remain within approximately ±10% of the baseline values.
Mechanical comparisons should be conducted under quasi-static loading at room temperature and 1000 °C, near a strain rate of 10^-3 s^-1, in an inert atmosphere.
The hypothesis does not extend to prolonged thermal exposure or long-term oxidation.

contradictions.description: The intervention says to replace roughly 20 atomic percent of Hf, which can mean 20 at.% of the whole alloy, whereas the experiment specifies approximately 20% of the Hf inventory. These imply very different Al concentrations.

The hypothesis assigns greater than 50% room-temperature ductility to HfMoTaTiZr, but the cited same-system evidence reports only 4% fracture strain for HfMoTaTiZr. The greater-than-50% value in that evidence pertains to a different composition before Mo addition.
